uncited: Application-Specific Extensions modify the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework to handle non-RGB, non-photometric data or to extract explicit geometry from the implicit volumetric representation [4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md], [5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md], [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md].

While standard 3DGS optimizes for novel-view synthesis of RGB scenes using calibrated camera poses and photometric losses, these adaptations replace the projection target with volumetric supervision, voxel-space rasterization, or 3D geometric intersections [5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md], [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md].

All extensions in this family retain the core 3DGS primitive representation: a set of $M$ anisotropic 3D Gaussian kernels $\mathcal{G} = \{G_i\}_{i=1}^M$ [4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md], [5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md].

In radiative and domain-specific variants, this is replaced by view-independent scalar attributes or feature vectors [4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md], [5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md].
3D Gaussian Splatting was originally introduced for real-time novel-view synthesis of RGB scenes [1795-3d-gaussian-splatting.md].
Radiative variants were developed to align the splatting model with X-ray physics [4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md].
Domain-specific adaptations were created to handle medical and microscopy data where volumetric supervision is more appropriate than photometric error [5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md].
Surface extraction methods address the inherent lack of explicit topology in the Gaussian representation [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md].
